topic: The Geometry of Light: Dandelin Spheres and Conic Sections
target_audience: High school geometry or early undergraduate students

sections.title: Prerequisite: The Cutting Plane
sections.content: Define a double cone and a cutting plane. Introduce the 'Conic Sections' (ellipse, parabola, hyperbola) based on the angle of intersection between the plane and the cone's axis.
sections.example: Use a flashlight beam against a wall: tilting the flashlight changes the shape of the light spot from a circle to an ellipse, then a parabola.

sections.title: Introducing the Dandelin Spheres
sections.content: Introduce the 'Dandelin Sphere'—a sphere placed inside the cone such that it is tangent to both the cone and the cutting plane. Explain the point of tangency.
sections.example: Imagine a bouncy ball trapped inside an ice cream cone, touching both the cone's inner walls and the glass lid placed at an angle.

sections.title: The Mathematical Magic: Proving the Ellipse
sections.content: Explain the key proof: The distance from any point on the intersection curve to the two tangency points (the foci) is constant. Use animation to show the equal tangent segments from a point to a sphere.
sections.example: Visualizing a string stretched between two pins (the foci) creating an ellipse, matching the distances to the Dandelin spheres.

sections.title: Connecting Shapes to Spheres
sections.content: Briefly describe how adding a second sphere allows us to generalize the proof for parabolas (one sphere) and hyperbolas (spheres in different nappes of the cone).
sections.example: A satellite dish (parabola) uses one sphere principle; a hourglass-shaped nuclear cooling tower (hyperboloid) uses two spheres.

sections.title: Summary and Real-world Synthesis
sections.content: Conclude by linking the abstract geometry of the spheres back to the physical properties of conic sections: focus, directrix, and eccentricity.
sections.example: Planetary orbits: Planets move in ellipses where the sun sits at one of the focal points defined by the Dandelin logic.
